The attached file ruth-matches.csv lists 12 DNA matches of one tester, coded M01–M12.

   shared_match_codes. A group is every match connected to the others through such links.

   form, merge or split groups.

- A list of bridge matches (from rule 4), or "none".

Here's a plan for recording your aunt's interview so you capture what she actually said, who prompted it, and how she agreed it could be used.

## 1. Before you record

**Get her consent first.** Tell her in plain words what you'll talk about, who will hear the recording, and how it may be used, for example "just for family" or "possibly a family-history society archive." Ask her to agree. Written, signed consent is best. Otherwise, record her saying yes at the start of the recording. Make sure she knows she can:
- skip any question
- take a break or stop at any time
- limit who hears the recording, or withdraw it later

Also tell her that once a recording is published or given to an archive, it may be impossible to take back fully.

**If her memory or understanding is uncertain:** explain things simply and let a trusted carer, relative or friend sit in, with their role agreed beforehand. That person is there to support her. Their agreement doesn't replace hers. If she can't understand and agree, the recording can only be a private family keepsake. Note that her agreement is missing, and never publish it or give it to an archive.

**Check the recording law where each of you is.** In the U.S., some states require everyone's consent, even for conversations in person. A phone call between states may fall under the stricter state's law. In the UK or EU, a recording of a living person counts as personal data once it goes beyond private household use. **Where do you and your aunt live?** Whatever the answer, record openly, with her consent on the recording.

## 2. Equipment

- Make a short test recording of both your voices and play it back.
- If possible, clip a lapel microphone on your aunt. Make sure your questions are recorded too, with a second mic or with the recorder placed between you. Later you'll need to tell what she said from what you suggested.
- Leave the recorder running for the whole session and watch the level meter. Use a phone as a backup if you can.
- Right after the session, check that it can be heard all the way through and copy it to a second place.

## 3. Asking questions

- **Start from something concrete:** a photo, an object, a recipe or an event she lived through.
- **With photos,** ask about the place, buildings, vehicles and season before asking who the people are. Never suggest a name ("Is that Grandpa Josef?"). If she names someone, write it down as *her* identification, with her reason. Don't decide who someone is because of a resemblance.
- **After an important question, stay quiet** and give her time to remember.
- **For older family stories,** ask about the oldest person she remembers from childhood. For each story she heard from someone else, note who told her, on what occasion, about how old she was, and how that person could have known.
- **Respect a "no."** If she seems to be straining to please you, stop and note that you stopped. Mark details that only came out after repeated pressing as "possibly reconstructed."
- **If another relative helps her remember** ("do you remember when…"), note who it was, what they said and roughly when in the recording. A detail that only the helper brought up is the helper's account, not hers.

# How to interview your aunt

The steps below follow the family-interview recipe in `recipes/family-interviews-and-oral-tradition.md`. That recipe has one main rule: treat everything your aunt says as **her account, to check later against records.** Don't enter it straight into your tree as fact.

## 1. Before the visit

- **Choose a topic and a few prompts.** Concrete things work better than open questions: a photograph, an object, a recipe, or an event your aunt lived through. A good opening question is "Who is the oldest person you remember from your childhood?" It tends to bring out stories that were passed down to her.
- **Check whether you're allowed to record.** Some U.S. states require everyone in a conversation to agree to being recorded, even face to face. In the UK and EU, a recording of a living person counts as personal data, and so does anything it says about other living relatives. Where do you and your aunt live? Tell me and I'll say what to check there. I can't tell you what the law requires.
- **Test your equipment.** If you can, clip a small lapel microphone on your aunt. Make sure your own questions are recorded too, using a second microphone or by putting the recorder between you. Record a short test of both voices and play it back. If you have a second device, run it as a backup.

## 2. Consent at the start

- Tell your aunt plainly what you'll talk about, who will hear the recording, and how it may be used, for example only within the family.
- Get her agreement in writing if possible. Otherwise, record her saying yes at the start of the recording.
- Tell her she can skip any question, take a break, stop altogether, or take back her agreement later.
- **Memory problems:** if you're not sure she understands who will hear the recording and how it will be used, explain it in plain words. You can also ask a carer or a relative she trusts to be there, with their role agreed beforehand. A carer saying yes is not the same as your aunt agreeing. If she can't really agree, keep the recording only as a private family memory, and never put it in an archive or publish it.

## 3. During the interview

- Keep the recorder running the whole time. Don't stop and restart it.
- **With a photograph,** ask about the place, the buildings, any cars and the season *before* asking who the people are. Never suggest a name you're hoping to hear. If she names someone, write it down as her identification and note why she thinks so. Don't name anyone yourself because they look alike.
- After an important question, **stay quiet** and give her time to remember.
- If someone else in the room prompts her ("Remember when…?"), write down who said it and when. A detail that only the other person brought up is that person's account, not hers.
- If a detail only comes out after you've pressed her several times, mark it as "possibly reconstructed." If she starts straining to please you, **stop** and make a note that you stopped.
- If she says "my grandmother told me…", record how the story reached her: who told her, on what occasion, how old she was then, and how that person could have known.

## 4. Afterwards

- The same day, check the file: can you hear everything, and is it complete? Then copy it somewhere else for safety.
- At the end, ask her to confirm how the recording may be used and note any limits she sets. Before you share it, let her listen to it or read a transcript if she can.
- Keep these four things separate: the **original recording** (never edited), your **transcript**, your **summary**, and **your own interpretation**. When you quote her, add the time in the recording. Mark words or names you couldn't make out as uncertain instead of guessing them into clean names.
- Keep a simple **session log**. For each session, note:
  - the date
  - who was there
  - how consent was given and any limits on use
  - the prompts you used
  - the file names
  - whether you stopped early, and why
- Then make one entry for each statement, noting who said it, who prompted it, and in which session.

## 5. Before sharing

Ask me again before you upload the recording, put it in an archive, send it to relatives, or add details about living people to an online tree. Once a recording is public or in an archive, it may be impossible to remove completely. Until then, keep the files on your own device.

**Two questions so I can tailor this:** Where do you and your aunt live? And what do you most want to learn from her? With answers to those, I can write a question list and suggest which photographs or documents to bring as prompts.

The opening rule and section 4 keep her statements as her account, attributed per session and statement, to check against records rather than enter into the tree as fact.

With a photograph, it asks about the place, buildings, cars and season before asking who the people are. It says 'Never suggest a name you're hoping to hear' and 'Don't name anyone yourself because they look alike,' so she recalls names without prompting.

In a possible half-sibling case, a first message that states the relationship is the most common way first contact goes badly. She may not know about a hidden pregnancy, an affair, an adoption or a donor. If you name the relationship, she has to react to a family secret before she has chosen to engage. >
> I'm trying to learn more about my own family background. [One factual sentence, e.g. "I was born in [place] in [year], and I know very little about my [father's / mother's] side."]
>
> Would you be willing to tell me [one question, e.g. "which part of your family has roots in [place]", or "your grandparents' names, if you're comfortable sharing them"]?

**No. The Find a Grave entry doesn't prove the death date.** It's a lead, and your copy already contains a conflict that needs resolving.

## What the memorial gives you

These are separate statements from separate sources. None of them is a reading of the stone you've checked yourself.

| Date | What it is | Source | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Death 12 March 1901 | The volunteer's database field | Memorial entry | The contributor's statement. Where they got it isn't shown. |
| Burial 15 March 1901 | The volunteer's database field | Memorial entry | A separate statement. It needs the cemetery or church burial register. |
| 13 March 1901 | A description of what the stone photo says | Attached photograph, as described | **Unread.** The transcription hasn't been checked against the image. |
| Death certificate or register | — | Not supplied | Not examined |
| Cemetery interment entry | — | Not supplied | Not examined |

## Why it isn't proof

- **A memorial isn't another witness.** At best it copies the stone. A contributor may have taken the date from an obituary, a family tree or nowhere at all. The date fields are the database's claim, not a reading of the stone, even when a photo is attached.
- **The 12th vs. 13th conflict stays open.** Don't pick one and don't average them. Common causes: a misread numeral, a stone carved years later from memory, a date taken from a newspaper notice, or one source giving the burial or registration date instead of the death date. Errors happen on stones as well as in databases.
- **The stone is also weak evidence on its own.** It may have been set long after 1901, using whatever date a relative remembered. If the stone, death certificate and obituary later agree, they may all come from the same family informant. In that case they count as one source, not three.
- **The burial date counts only as a burial date.** Keep 15 March as its own fact. Don't use it to fill or check the death date until a burial register confirms it.

## What would actually settle it

1. **Read the photo yourself.** On the memorial, open every gallery image with **View original**. Read the stone before you look at the database dates again. Note the image's pixel size and what you can and can't make out at that size, and whether the letters look traced or painted in. If you share the image here, I can help read it.
2. **Get the civil death registration** for the place and year. This is the record that normally answers the question, and its death date usually comes from someone who was present at or near the death. The place matters: which country or U.S. state? In 1901 many U.S. states didn't yet register deaths statewide, which changes where you'd look.
3. **Get the cemetery's interment register** (sexton or cemetery office). It tests the 15 March burial and often gives a death date and plot number too. If the burial was in a churchyard, the church burial register is the equivalent.
4. **Look for a contemporary death notice or obituary.** It's useful, but it may come from the same family informant as the stone.
5. **Write down the result whatever it is.** If the stone, the register and the certificate still disagree, keep all three dates, each with its source, and judge them by who supplied the information and how close that person was to the death. Don't just go with the majority.

If you think about messaging the memorial's contributor about the photo or their source, that means contacting a living stranger and revealing your research interest. We'd go through the privacy checklist first. I haven't contacted anyone.

**To narrow down step 2, where did this person die (country, and state or county if it was in the U.S.)?**

# Proving your 4th great-grandfather's parents

Most ancestors from that era have no single record that names their parents. Usually the proof is a written argument: several independent records point to one couple, the conflicts are explained, and other candidates are ruled out. The plan below is a general method. Which record collections to search depends on details I don't have yet (questions at the end).

## 1. State exactly what you're proving
Write it as one sentence, for example: "[Name], born about [year] in [place], was the son of [father] and [mother]." Separate your known facts (what records actually say) from your assumptions, such as "he was the eldest son" or "the same mother had all the children."

## 2. Build a record-by-record table for him
Find every record of his own life: birth or baptism, marriage, children's baptisms, census entries, land, tax, will or estate, death and burial. Give each record one row and each identifying detail its own column: dates, places, spouse, children, occupation, neighbours, witnesses, godparents, signature or mark. Sort the table by those details, not by name. A shared name is the weakest evidence of identity.

For each statement, ask whether the person who supplied it knew it firsthand. A death record's informant usually knew the death firsthand, but not the parents' names.

## 3. Treat the proposed parents as a hypothesis, with rivals
- Write down where the proposed parents came from. Five online trees repeating one claim count as one unverified claim, not five witnesses.
- Keep at least one other possibility open, including "parents unknown."
- **Search for namesakes.** Look for other men with his name, and other couples with the proposed parents' names, in the same place and period. Count them and list each one. Keep each candidate's records in a separate file so they don't get mixed together.

## 4. Search the records that can link a child to parents
Depending on country and period, these typically include:
- His own baptism or birth entry.
- His marriage record. Some forms name parents, and a later remarriage may ask for them when the first marriage didn't.
- The proposed parents' wills, estate files, deeds of gift, heirs' deeds and guardianships. Remember an heir list is not a list of all children, and a will can leave out a child already provided for.
- Census entries that give relationships.
- Associates: godparents, marriage witnesses, sureties, neighbours and land next door. These often reveal family ties that no record states directly.

## 5. Run reality checks
- Was the mother of childbearing age at his birth?
- Was the father alive, or dead no more than about ten months before the birth?
- Could the family really have been in each recorded place, given the distances and travel of the time?

A true impossibility rules the link out. Softer oddities are conflicts to investigate, not automatic disproof.

## 6. Include a search that could disprove the link
Name in advance what result would count against it. For example:
- A baptism of a same-named boy to a different couple in that parish.
- A burial showing the proposed parents' son of that name died as a child.
- A same-named man in the area whose details fit your ancestor better.
- An estate settlement of the proposed father that names heirs incompatible with your ancestor.

"No record found" counts as evidence only after you've confirmed the record should exist, survives, and was covered by the index or images you searched. Log every search with its date.

## 7. DNA, if you use it
For a parent link this far back, you'd compare with descendants of the proposed parents through your ancestor's siblings. Those people are roughly your 6th cousins, so DNA evidence is thin at this distance. Each match counts only once that tester's descent to the couple is documented generation by generation. You'd then want several independent descendant lines that agree with the paper trail. If a direct male line survives on both sides, a Y-DNA comparison can test the paternal link. It can't show in which generation the shared ancestor lived.

## 8. Write the argument
Write a step-by-step correlation: what each record says, how they fit together, why conflicts arose, and why the rivals were ruled out. You make the final call on whether it's proven, not me or any other AI tool.

---

**To turn this into actual record collections, please tell me:**
1. His name, approximate birth and death years, and where he lived (country and county/region or parish).
2. His religion, if known.
3. Who the proposed parents are, and where that claim comes from (a tree, family Bible, compiled book, DNA hint).
4. Which records you already have for him.

If you later bring in DNA match data from other people, ask them before sharing it with any tool or site.

- Baptism or birth entries
- Marriage entries or licences that name parents

I can't give you a reliable probability that she's your second cousin, and I won't calculate one myself. A percentage that an AI computes from a cM figure is made up, and the recipes I follow treat it as a hard rule not to do that. Below is what 212 cM can and can't tell you, and how to get a properly sourced figure.

## What 212 cM tells you

- **It fits several relationships.** 212 cM is a typical amount for second cousins, but it is also typical for other relationships that share about the same amount of DNA. Those include first cousins twice removed, half first cousins once removed and half great-grand-aunt or great-grand-niece, plus some nearby half or removed relationships. The amount alone can't separate relationships that share the same expected cM. Half and full relationships often can't be told apart by cM either.
- **The common ancestor could be in different generations.** For a second cousin, the shared ancestors are your great-grandparents. For a first cousin twice removed, they are one generation higher in the younger person's tree and one generation lower in the older person's tree. Search every depth that a candidate relationship implies, in both trees.

## Getting a sourced probability

Enter **212** in DNA Painter's Shared cM tool (https://dnapainter.com/tools/sharedcmv4). Keep the whole candidate list it returns, not just the top line, and note these limits:

1. **Probabilities cover groups.** The tool gives one probability for a group of relationships that share about the same amount, for example second cousin together with first cousin twice removed. That figure is not the chance of "second cousin" alone.
2. **They are based on AncestryDNA data.** On 2026-10-23 the tool credited its probabilities to The DNA Geek's statistics, which come from an AncestryDNA white paper. If your 212 cM came from Ancestry, check whether it is the weighted or unweighted amount. If you have both, run each one and label the results by input. If the 212 came from another company, the probabilities are not calibrated for it, so note that.
3. **The histogram percentages are not probabilities.** The histogram for "2C" shows where 212 falls among reported second-cousin pairs. It doesn't show how likely it is that she is a second cousin.

Privacy: enter only the number. Don't type her name or any other details into the tool.

| Field | Value | Effect |
|---|---|---|

Proving the parents of a 4th great-grandfather usually means building a written argument from several records. A single record that states the relationship is rare at that distance. Here's the method. Which actual record collections to search depends on where and when he lived, which you haven't said yet.

## The method

**1. Pin down the question.** Write it as one claim, for example "John X (born about 1790, Place Y) was the son of A and B." Decide up front that the standard is a reasoned, documented argument with conflicts explained. It is not certainty, and it is not agreement among online trees.

**2. Check what you already "know".** List every source behind his current parents. Five online trees copying one claim count as one unverified claim. For each record, ask three things:
- Is it an original, an index or transcription, or a compiled book?
- Did the informant have firsthand knowledge of *this particular fact*?
- Does it state the relationship directly, or only imply it?

If the link rests on trees, record hints or a book that doesn't cite its sources, treat it as unproven. Stop building upward from it until it's tested.

**3. Make sure the records are all about him before looking for his parents.** Put every record you have for him in a table, one row per record. Give each detail its own column: dates, places, spouse, children, occupation, neighbours, witnesses, land, and signature or mark. Then sort by those columns, not by name. A shared name is the weakest link between two records.

**4. Look for direct evidence first.** These record types often name a man's parents:
- his baptism or birth entry
- his marriage entry, where the form asked for parents
- his death record (but the informant usually knew his parents only secondhand)
- a parent's will or estate file naming him as a son
- deeds between family members, guardianship records, or church removal papers

**5. If nothing states it, build an indirect argument and write it out.** Chain together clues that fit only one family: estate shares, land passing to him, the same witnesses and sponsors, neighbours who moved with the family, and household make-up across censuses or tax lists. Naming patterns can suggest where to search next. They are not evidence of parentage.

**6. Search for namesakes on purpose.** List everyone with his name in that place and period. Also list every other son the proposed parents could have had with the same name, and other couples with the proposed parents' names. Rule a candidate out only on positive evidence, for example a matching burial in childhood or a documented family elsewhere. If one candidate survives, that doesn't make him your man. You still need a detail that separates him from a namesake you haven't found, such as age, spouse, place or household.

**7. Run at least one search that could disprove the link.** Write down what would refute it and which record would show it. Examples:
- the proposed father's will or estate names his children and leaves out your ancestor, with no gift during his lifetime to explain it
- a burial shows the proposed son died as a child
- your ancestor's own later records give a different birthplace or different parents
- the dates are impossible, such as a mother past childbearing age or a birth more than about ten months after the father's death

"No record found" counts as evidence only if the records covered that place and period, survive, are indexed (or you browsed them), and should have included him. Log every search with its date.

**8. Use DNA as one part of the same argument.** His parents are your 6th great-grandparents, so many genuine cousins at that distance share little or no DNA. DNA helps most as supporting evidence: matches who descend from *other* children of the proposed parents, each with a documented paper descent first. Judge matches by quality, not by how many there are. Don't read a cM figure as giving relationship odds. Endogamy can inflate shared DNA. Before uploading a kit, exporting match lists or contacting a match, the privacy steps for living testers apply, and I'd go through them with you first.

**9. Keep the working hypothesis separate from proof.** While you test "A is his father," treat A's own parents as *conditional* grandparents, not established ones. If that premise fails, recheck everything that depends on it.

**10. Write the proof summary.** It should state the claim, the evidence, how the records correlate, how each conflict is resolved, and what remains uncertain. I can help assemble and draft it, but you decide whether it actually meets the standard.

## To choose actual records

**Where and roughly when did he live, and what is your current source for his parents?** Give the country, region or county, approximate birth and death years, and religion if known. The source might be a tree, a book, a record or family tradition. The place and period decide which registers, probate courts, censuses or tax lists exist and survive.

# How to prove your 4th great-grandfather's parents

You prove parents with one written argument: several independent records that point to the same couple, any conflicts between them explained, and other candidates ruled out. Five records that agree are not enough on their own. The method below works anywhere. Which records you search depends on where and when he lived.

## 1. Frame the question and write down what you already know
- **The question:** for example, "Who were the parents of [name], born about [year] in [place]?" Decide whether you are testing parents someone has already proposed, such as in an online tree, or starting with no candidates.
- **Your evidence so far:** list each record you hold and what it says about him. For each fact, note who supplied it and whether that person knew it firsthand. A death record's informant usually knew the death firsthand but the birth only secondhand.
- **Copies count once:** online trees that copy each other are one unverified claim, not several witnesses. Treat a tree as a lead, never as evidence.

## 2. Build an identity file before linking him to any parents
- Make a table with one row per record about him. Add columns for every detail it gives: dates, places, spouse, children, occupation, neighbours, witnesses, godparents, and whether he signed or made a mark.
- **Search for other men with the same name** in the same place and period, and for other couples with the proposed parents' names. Give each of these namesakes his own table, so records about one don't drift into another man's file. Finding only one candidate doesn't prove he's the right one. Name a detail that would tell him apart from a namesake you haven't found yet.
- **Check what's possible.** A mother past childbearing age, or a birth more than about ten months after the father's death, rules a couple out. Smaller oddities are conflicts to investigate, not grounds to rule a couple out.

## 3. Look for records that state the relationship, then build up indirect evidence
- **Records that may name his parents directly**, depending on the place: his baptism or birth entry, his marriage entry, his death record, or a parent's will or estate papers naming him.
- **If no record states it**, as often happens before about 1850, use indirect evidence:
  - wills, estate distributions and deeds that tie him to the proposed family
  - land passing between them
  - neighbours, associates and witnesses they share
  - godparents or sureties from the proposed family
  - a pattern in how his children were named (this can only suggest where to search next)
  - the proposed parents' household in a census or tax list, with someone of his age in it

  You then have to write out how these clues fit together. An indirect conclusion is never proved just by stating it.

## 4. Run a search that could prove the proposed parents wrong
- Write the proposed parents down as a working hypothesis, alongside the main alternative, which may simply be "unknown parents". Note what each one predicts you would find.
- Choose at least one record that would disprove the link if the parents were wrong. For example, the proposed parents' will or estate papers may list their children without him, or the namesake may turn out to have the same parents.
- **"No record found" is a search result, not evidence.** A missing record only counts once you've confirmed that the records survive, that the collection covers that place and those years, and that the index isn't simply missing the entry. Log every search with its date.

## 5. Use DNA as part of the same argument
At five generations back, autosomal DNA can support a paper case, but only if two conditions hold. First, you must have documented every parent-to-child link from each DNA match down to the proposed parents. Second, the DNA and the paper trail must point to the same couple. Matches through the proposed parents' other children work best. A Y-DNA test of a direct-male-line descendant can test a paternal link. What you need is matches you can trace with records, not a long list of matches.

## 6. Write the proof and make the decision yourself
Write a summary that:
- sets out each piece of evidence
- explains every conflict
- describes the namesakes you ruled out and why
- lists what is still uncertain

You decide whether the argument is strong enough. It's fine to label the parents "probable" or to leave the question unresolved.

# How to interview your 90-year-old aunt

The goal is a recording that is still usable later. That means you can always tell what she said, what someone asked her and who suggested a detail. Everything she tells you is her account. It's not a fact for your tree until records support it.

## 1. Before the visit

- **Tell her the plan.** Explain what you want to talk about, who will hear the recording and how you might use it, for example "just the family" or "possibly an archive someday." Get her consent. Written consent is best. Otherwise, start the recording by asking her to agree out loud.
- **Check the recording law where each of you is.** In the U.S., some states require everyone's consent, even for conversations in person. If you interview her by phone across state lines, the stricter state's rule may apply. In the UK or EU, a recording of a living person counts as personal data. Record openly either way.
- **Think about her memory honestly.** If you doubt she can understand who will hear the recording, use plain words and invite a trusted relative or carer she knows. Agree on that person's role in advance. Their agreement doesn't replace hers. If she can't really agree, keep any recording for private family memory only. Never deposit or publish it.
- **Choose a few concrete prompts** instead of broad questions like "tell me about the family." Good prompts include:
  - an old photograph
  - an object, such as a dish, tool or piece of jewellery
  - a family recipe
  - a specific event she lived through
  - her own entry in an old census. Read out the neighbours listed before and after her household and ask what she remembers about them.
  - "Who was the oldest person you remember from your childhood?" This often brings out stories from a generation further back.

## 2. Equipment

- Clip a lapel microphone on her. Make sure your questions are recorded too, with a second mic or with the recorder placed between you. Later you'll need to hear exactly what was asked.
- Make a short test recording of both voices and play it back before you start.
- If you can, run a phone as a backup recorder.
- Let the recorder run for the whole session. Don't stop and restart it. Splitting into files of about an hour is fine.

## 3. During the interview

- **With a photograph,** ask about the cars, buildings, place and season before you ask who the people are. Never suggest a name, even one you're hoping to hear. If she names someone, record that as her identification and note the reason she gives.
- **After an important question, stay quiet** and give her time to remember.
- **Let her set limits.** She can skip a question, take a break, stop or later restrict access to the recording.
- **If a relative helps her remember** ("Do you remember when…?"), note who said it and what they said. A detail that only the helper mentioned is the helper's account, not hers.
- **Don't push.** If an answer only comes after repeated pressing, or she seems to be straining to please you, stop. Note why you stopped, and mark that detail "possibly reconstructed."
- **For stories she heard from others,** ask who told her, when, how old she was then and how that person could have known.

## 4. Afterwards

- **Check the file the same day.** Make sure every part can be heard, then copy it somewhere else. If an answer is missing or inaudible, write that down. Don't fill it in from the question you asked.
- **Ask her to confirm how the recording may be used,** ideally with a signed release form. A short joint statement you both fill in also works. Note any restrictions. If possible, let her listen to the recording or read the transcript before anyone else does.
- **Keep the original audio untouched.** Your transcript, summaries and interpretations are separate layers. Write down the time in the recording for any quote or name you're unsure of, so you can replay it. Mark unclear names as unclear instead of guessing a spelling.
- **Keep the files on your own device for now.** Before you upload them to a family-history app, cloud folder or archive, or share them with relatives, we'll go through the privacy checklist together. Her recording will also mention other living relatives.

## 5. Records to keep

**A session register, one row per session:**
- the date, place and everyone present
- how and when she gave consent, the agreed topic and who may hear the recording
- whether she has authorized sharing (release form, joint statement, recorded statement, or not yet), with any restrictions
- any carer or helper present and their role
- the prompts or items used

# Interviewing your 90-year-old aunt

An interview gives you her account of the family. Record it so that later you can tell what she said, what someone asked her, and what was suggested to her. Nothing she says should go straight into your tree as a fact.

## 1. Before the session
- **Consent.** Tell her in plain words what you'd like to talk about, who will hear the recording, and how it may be used (private family memory, shared with cousins, or deposited in an archive). Get her agreement in writing if possible. If not, record her spoken agreement at the start of the recording. Tell her she can skip any question, take a break, stop, limit who hears it, or withdraw it later.
- **Her understanding.** If you doubt she can follow who will hear it and how it will be used, for example because of memory loss, explain simply and let a trusted carer or relative sit in, with that person's role agreed beforehand. A carer's agreement does not replace hers. If she can't give informed agreement, keep any recording for private family memory only, note in your records that her own agreement is missing, and never deposit or publish it.
- **Recording law.** Check the rules where each of you will be. Some U.S. states require every party's consent, including in person and on calls across state lines. In the UK and EU, a recording of a living person counts as personal data once it goes beyond private household use. Record openly and capture her consent on the recording.
- **Equipment.** Clip a lapel microphone on her. Make sure your questions are recorded too, with a second mic or the recorder placed between you. Do a short test of both voices and play it back. Run a second device as a backup if you can.
- **Prompts.** Pick a few specific things to talk about: a photograph, an object, a recipe, or an event she lived through. Open-ended questions about "the family history" work less well.

## 2. During the session
- **Keep the recorder running** the whole time instead of stopping and restarting it. Watch the level meter.
- **With photographs,** ask about the cars, buildings, place and season before asking who the people are. Never suggest a name you're hoping to hear. If she names someone, write it down as her identification, along with her reason. Don't decide who someone is by how they look.
- **With a census page** from her childhood, show her own household's entry, read out the neighbours listed before and after it, and ask what she remembers. Living next door on the page doesn't prove two families were related.
- **Ask about the oldest person she remembers from childhood.** This often brings out stories passed down in the family. For any story she heard from someone else, ask who told her, when, how old she was then, and how that person would have known.
- **After an important question, stay quiet** and give her time to remember.
- **If another relative helps her** ("do you remember when…"), note who said what. Anything that relative introduced is the relative's account, not hers.
- **Stop if she starts straining to give you answers.** Note that you stopped. Mark anything that only came out after repeated pressing as "possibly reconstructed".
- **If she doesn't want to discuss a topic,** let it go.

## 3. Afterwards
- Check the file right away: can you hear both voices, and did it record the whole session? Copy it to a second place you control. If an answer wasn't recorded or can't be heard, note the gap. Don't fill it in from the question you asked.
- Ask her to confirm the terms of use, ideally with a signed release or a simple joint statement you both fill in. If she'd like to, let her review the recording or transcript before anyone else hears it.
- Keep three things separate: the unedited recording, your transcript (with time offsets for quotes and unclear names, marked as uncertain rather than tidied up), and your own interpretation.
- Keep three records:
  - **Session register:** who was present, date, consent and sharing terms, the prompts used, files, and any stop.
  - **Statement record:** who said each thing, who prompted it, and which session it first came from.
  - **Chain record:** for each story passed down, who told it to whom.
- Use documents to check her dates and the order of events. If she gets the order wrong, that doesn't make the events themselves wrong.

**Before sharing:** the recording can stay on your own device without any further checks. Sharing it with relatives, uploading it to an app or tree site, or depositing it in an archive counts as moving her data and that of living relatives she mentions. Get her confirmation and go through the privacy checklist first. Once a recording has gone to an archive or been published, it may be impossible to remove fully, so tell her that before it leaves the family.

To tailor this further, can you tell me where she lives and whether you'll interview her in person or by phone or video? That decides which recording rules apply. It would also help to know which family questions you most hope she can answer, so I can suggest specific prompts.

# Interviewing your aunt: a practical plan

A recording of your aunt is a source in its own right. It is also a record of a living person's voice and memories, which may include things about other living relatives. Most of the work is setting it up so that later you can tell what she said, what someone else suggested to her, and what you concluded from it.

## 1. Before the visit

**Agree consent with her first.** Before you start recording, tell her three things in plain words:
- the topic (for example, "your childhood and your parents' family")
- who will hear the recording (for example, "just me and my sister")
- how it might be used (for example, "for our family tree, kept privately")

Ask whether she agrees. A signed note is best. Otherwise, say it again once the recorder is running and let her answer on the recording. Tell her she can skip any question, take a break, stop altogether, limit who hears it, or withdraw it later.

**If her memory or understanding is uncertain:** explain everything simply and invite a carer or relative she trusts to sit in, with their role agreed beforehand. Their agreement doesn't replace hers. If she can't really agree, keep the recording only as private family memory. Note that her own agreement is missing, and never deposit or publish it.

**Check recording law where each of you is.** Some U.S. states require everyone's consent, including for in-person conversations. A phone call across state lines can fall under the stricter state's rule. In the UK and EU, the recording is personal data about her and about any living people she names. Purely household use is exempt, but sharing or publishing may not be. I can't tell you which rule applies, so please check yours. Recording openly, with her consent captured at the start, avoids most of the problem.

**Equipment:**
- Make a short test recording of both your voices and play it back.
- Clip a lapel microphone on her. Make sure your questions are recorded too, with a second mic or with the recorder between you. Later you'll need to hear exactly what was asked.
- Run a second device as a backup if you can.

**Gather prompts.** Concrete prompts work better than open questions with a 90-year-old: old photographs, an object, a family recipe, or a census page from her childhood.

## 2. During the session

- **Keep the recorder running the whole time.** Don't stop and restart it, and keep an eye on the level meter. If the recorder splits the file every hour or so, that's fine.
- **With photographs, ask about the setting before the people.** Ask about the cars, buildings, place and season first, then "who's this?" Never suggest the name you hope to hear. If she names someone, record it as her identification and note her reason. Don't decide who someone is by resemblance.
- **A census page makes a good neighbourhood prompt.** Show her her own household's entry, read out the neighbours listed before and after it, and ask what she remembers about them. Being listed next door doesn't prove the neighbours were relatives.
- **Ask about the oldest person she remembers from childhood.** This often brings out stories passed down from earlier generations. For any story she heard rather than saw, ask who told her, when, roughly how old she was, and how that person would have known.
- **Leave silences after important questions.** Let her think instead of filling the pause.
- **Respect topics she doesn't want to discuss.**
- **Don't press.** If she seems to be straining to help you, stop and note that you stopped. Details that appear only after repeated questions should be flagged as possibly reconstructed.
- **Note any prompting by other relatives.** If someone else in the room says "do you remember when…", record who said it and the wording, or the time on the recording. Details that only the prompter mentioned are the prompter's account, not your aunt's.

At her age, several shorter visits may tire her less than one long one; that's general advice rather than part of the method. If you do return, note which session first produced each detail.

## 3. Right after

- Check the file is complete and audible, then copy it to a second place on your own storage.
- Ask her to confirm the terms of use. A signed release is best, or a recorded statement, or a simple joint statement of intent you both fill in. Note any restrictions. Offer to let her listen to the recording or read the transcript before anyone else does.
- Keep the original file unedited. Keep three things separate: the recording, your transcript (with times for quotes and unclear passages, and unclear names marked as uncertain), and your own interpretation.

## 4. Afterwards: what to keep

- **The unedited recording(s).** If part of a conversation wasn't recorded, write a separate dated note of it.
- **A session register** for each session: who was present, the date, her consent and the agreed terms, any restrictions, any carer and their role, the prompts used, the file names, and any point where you stopped.
- **A statement record:** who said each thing, who prompted it, and whether it is her words, your transcript, a paraphrase or your interpretation.
- **A chain record** for any story she heard from someone else.

**Don't enter her memories in the tree as facts yet.** Each one is her account, to be checked against records. A remembered date or relationship can be the best lead you have, and it still needs documentary support.

Sharing the recording with relatives outside your household, uploading it to an app or tree site, or depositing it in an archive is a separate step. Before doing any of that, work through her permission, who would see it, and what it says about other living people. Tell me when you get there and we'll go through it together.

Would it help if I drafted a short consent script, or a set of photo and neighbourhood prompts suited to where and when she grew up? Tell me roughly where and when that was.

# How to prove your 4th great-grandfather's parents

There's no single record that settles this for every family. Which records exist depends on where and when he lived. The method is the same everywhere, though: you build one written argument that ties his parents to him and rules out other candidates. Here is the plan, with the record choices left open until I know his place and period.

## 1. State exactly what you're trying to prove
Write it as one sentence, for example: *"John Doe, born about 1790, who married Mary Roe and was the father of [your 3rd great-grandparent], was the son of A and B."* That sentence contains two separate things to prove:
- **His identity.** You need to know which man in the records is *your* John, using details beyond his name.
- **The parent-child link.** You need evidence connecting that particular man to A and B.

Before you work on his parents, check the generations below him. If the link between him and his child is weak, fix that first. Anything you build above a shaky link is only conditional.

## 2. Collect every record of *him*, working backward from his death
Make a table with one row per record and one column per detail: event date and recording date, place, age, occupation, spouse, children, neighbours, witnesses, and whether he signed or made a mark. Death, probate, land, tax, census, church and court records often give clues about his parents indirectly: a birthplace, a sibling acting as witness, or land passed down from a father. Sort the table by each detail, not by name.

## 3. Look for other men with the same name
Search for every man with his name, and every couple with the proposed parents' names, in that place and period. Keep each candidate in a separate file so their records don't get mixed together. Rule a candidate out only on positive evidence. "I found no later record of him" doesn't eliminate anyone. And if only one candidate is left, he is still just a candidate. You need a detail that would tell him apart from a namesake you haven't found, such as age, place, spouse or household.

## 4. Look for direct evidence, but expect to rely on indirect evidence
For his generation, the strongest sources are usually:
- the candidate father's **will or probate file**, or the heirs listed in an intestate estate (keep in mind that heirs are not the same as a list of children)
- **deeds** passing land from father to son, or heirs selling land together
- **guardianship** records, if he was a minor when his father died
- his **baptism** entry
- **tax lists**, read year by year, showing when he appears as a separate taxpayer

A record that only *mentions* both men doesn't prove they were father and son. If no record says so directly, you have to write out how the clues fit together.

## 5. Weigh sources, don't count them
Ten online trees that copy each other are one unproven claim. For each fact, ask who supplied it and whether that person could have known it firsthand. A death certificate's informant usually knew the death firsthand but the birth only secondhand. A headstone, a death certificate and an obituary often all go back to the same relative. If records conflict, explain why before you pick a value.

## 6. Test at least two explanations, not just your favourite
- **H1:** A and B were his parents.
- **H2:** another couple, or another man of the same name, fits better.
- **H3:** his parents are unknown.

For each, write down what you would expect to find if it were true. Then choose a search that could prove H1 wrong. For example, check whether A's will or estate leaves out a son of the right age, or whether A's household had no boy of the right age. A list of sources that only confirm H1 doesn't test it.

## 7. Use DNA only as part of the same argument
At this distance, a DNA match descending from his parents would usually be a 5th cousin or more distant. Such a match counts as evidence only after you have documented the match's line, parent by parent, down from the proposed couple. The paper trail and the DNA then have to point to the same answer. One good match beats many weak ones. If he is on your direct paternal line, Y-DNA tests from documented descendants of A's other sons can be a strong check.

## 8. Write the argument down, and make the call yourself
The result is a written proof: the records, how reliable each one is, how the conflicts are resolved, how the rival candidates were ruled out, and how the indirect clues fit together. If you can't explain and defend each step from the records, the link isn't proved yet.

---

**To pick specific record collections:** where and roughly when was he born and living, and what records do you already have about him and the parents you think are his? The country, region and religion decide which registers and court records exist, and whether they survive.

Put every record of his adult life in a table, one row per record. Give dates, places, spouse, children, occupation, neighbours, signature or mark, and land each their own column. Then sort by each column, not by name. Similar names are the weakest evidence you have. A biologically or chronologically impossible timeline blocks a merge. Smaller oddities are conflicts to investigate.

## 3. Look for direct statements, and judge each one separately
Depending on the place and period, these might be:
- a baptism or birth entry naming the parents
- a marriage record naming his parents
- a parent's will, estate distribution or guardianship naming him as a son
- a deed between him and a parent that states the relationship
- a death record. Its informant usually knew the death firsthand but the parents only secondhand.

Judge each statement by who supplied it and what that person could have known. Five trees that copy one claim count as one claim. If you're working from an index or transcript, find the original image.

Many fourth-great-grandparents fall in this gap. You chain clues into an explicit argument:
- **Household:** placement before he married (e.g. U.S. censuses before 1850 give only the head's name)
- **Land:** land passing from the parent to him, or shared with siblings
- **People around him:** sponsors, witnesses and bondsmen
- **Migration:** moving with the candidate family
- **Naming patterns:** a lead only, never the basis of the case

A record that just mentions him alongside the candidates doesn't prove they were his parents. Write out why each clue points to this couple.

## 5. Search for rivals deliberately
- Search the same place and period for other men with your ancestor's name, and for other couples named A and B.
- Record each search: the collection, the query, the number of results and the date.

Write down what would refute it, and which record could show that. For example:
- A and B's son of that name was buried as a child.
- That son appears elsewhere with a different wife.
- Your ancestor is missing from the father's estate distribution while all the other children are named.

Before you count a missing entry as evidence, rule out lost records, gaps in coverage and indexing errors. "No record found" is only a search result.

At this distance, DNA tests a hypothesis; it doesn't prove one. The most useful matches descend from **other children** of A and B, or from A's or B's siblings.

Clustering and comparing hypotheses are covered by the unknown-parentage/WATO workflow if you get that far.

## 8. Write it up and decide yourself

- the records and what each one says
- how you resolved each conflict
- which rivals you eliminated and how
- the searches that came up empty, with dates

5. **Upgrade to narrow the range.** Going from Y-37 to Y-111 to Big Y-700 narrows it, but only if he also tests. Big Y-700 is the test that can tell a recent Smith connection from a deep coincidence, and FTDNA's Match Time Tree dates your shared branch, still as a range.
6. **Compare your documented paper trails.** Look at the earliest known Smith ancestor and place in each tree. Only records can name the common ancestor. Until they do, treat the match as a lead.

If you share the TiP range, each man's test level and the differing marker values, I can help you read them.

DUTCH-CIVIL-CHURCH-RECORD-RECOVERY-01.quote: A failed search on WieWasWie or Open Archieven (openarchieven.nl) does not show that the event is missing from the municipality's records.

EARLY-NEW-ENGLAND-TOWN-RECORDS-01.quote: **Never report "not in the town records" without the coverage behind it.** Name the towns, volumes and page ranges actually read, and the volumes not read.

ELIB-UKRAINIAN-ARCHIVE-REFERENCE-BOOKS-0.quote: Prefer the current card's link over a constructed URL. A constructed route is a retrieval lead until its response is verified as the intended PDF; redirects, error HTML or an access failure leave acquisition unresolved.

ENGLAND-WALES-GRO-INDEX-RECOVERY-01.quote: These entries tell you the registration quarter, district, volume/page and, in the GRO birth index, the mother's maiden surname. They do not give an event date, a birthplace, a pairing of spouses or parentage.

ENGLISH-NONREGISTER-RECORD-RECOVERY-01.quote: Record which series do not cover the case. The register being silent does not make the question unanswerable.

ENSLAVEMENT-RECORD-DISCLOSURE-01.quote: Prepare an extract that preserves the names as written and gives a locator for the original.

ETHNICITY-ESTIMATE-VERSION-COMPARISON-01.quote: The tester's DNA did not change between versions; the vendor's method did. Ask first what the vendor changed, not what changed in the family [S11].

EVIDENCE-PROOF-JUDGMENT-01.quote: **You rule on identity and proof. The model assembles and drafts — it never concludes.**

PROOF-01.quote: **You rule on identity and proof. The model assembles and drafts — it never concludes.**

PROOF-02.quote: **Keep same-name candidates in SEPARATE research projects** so their records never cross-contaminate.

PROOF-03.quote: A converged match is evidence in the proof argument, not proof by itself.

PROOF-04.quote: **Include a search that challenges the preferred version.**

FAMILY-ARCHIVES-MATERIAL-STORAGE-01.quote: Record what was kept together before rehousing any item.

FAMILY-COLLECTION-INTAKE-AND-CAPTURE-01.quote: The common mistake is to optimize for tidy files. The model renames files by person, re-orders items, scans fronts only, imposes one resolution or format, treats a received crop or a stitched assembly as the master, and assumes an export kept the captions. Each of those destroys part of the record that later identification depends on: who held the item, the order it arrived in, its reverse, and the surfaces nobody has inspected yet.

FAMILY-INTERVIEWS-AND-ORAL-TRADITION-01.quote: A correctly recorded recollection remains an account to assess, not an automatic tree fact.

ORAL-01.quote: Before a new recording starts, explain the topic, who will hear the recording and how it may be used, and get the participant's consent.

ORAL-02.quote: With a photograph, ask about the vehicles, buildings, place and season before asking who the people are, and never supply a desired identity [S2].

FAMILY-PAPERS-AND-BIBLE-REGISTER-DATING-.quote: A postmark dates the mailing. It is the latest possible date for the writing and for any event the text reports as already past, but it does not date those events: a birth, death, visit or move reported inside a card needs its own date [S1].

FAMILY-PHOTOGRAPH-ATTRIBUTION-AND-DATING.quote: record each identification as an attributed claim with its basis, turn every clue into an earliest or latest bound, and test an attribution against the documented lifetime of the person named, never against faces.

PHOTO-01.quote: Preserve the attribution and its basis; do not identify a person by their face or compare faces across photographs.

PHOTO-02.quote: Before you upload a private family photograph to any outside service (reverse image search, enhancement or colorization), answer the privacy gate in `SKILL.md` and get the user's explicit permission for that service.

FAMILYSEARCH-PRACTICAL-RECORD-WORKFLOWS-.quote: Confirm candidates from the image and context. A name appearing in text does not establish the candidate's identity.

FIND-A-GRAVE-MEMORIAL-CORRECTIONS-01.quote: Select the correction or management action from the memorial itself.

FRENCH-BELGIAN-CIVIL-ACT-EXTRACTION-01.quote: Store two fields: the act date, and the event date as stated (literal) or as resolved. Never fill only one date field.

FRENCH-CANADIAN-REGISTER-RECOVERY-01.quote: Do not call the person absent until the name forms are exhausted

FRENCH-DEPARTMENTAL-RECORD-ROUTING-01.quote: **Send each search to an Archives départementales (AD), not to a national index.** Older civil registers, census lists, military registers, Enregistrement tables and notarial minutes are kept by the AD, each with its own website and series.

FTDNA-PRACTICAL-DNA-WORKFLOWS-01.quote: A match name is a join key, not a unique person identifier. Matching Bucket and Linked Relationship are values observed at download. Record link changes separately from the retrieval date, keep the export choice and kit with the rows, and refresh match metadata after relinking.

FTM-RESEARCH-WORKFLOWS-01.quote: Treat a FamilySearch branch, a Web Search result and a relative's sticky note as leads to check against records, never as facts for the research file.

FTM-RESEARCH-WORKFLOWS-02.quote: Rolling back returns the tree to its state before the selected action and deletes every later change

FTM-RESEARCH-WORKFLOWS-05.quote: Run it only for people known to be deceased.

FTM-RESEARCH-WORKFLOWS-06.quote: Do not import the address book and do not look up anyone's email address

GALICIA-BUKOVINA-HABSBURG-RECORD-ROUTING.quote: **Start an ethnic Ukrainian villager in Galicia in Greek Catholic books, not Orthodox ones.**

GEDCOM-RESEARCH-EXPORT-01.quote: The recipe prevents seven failures: changing the header version and calling the file converted, attaching a child to the father's wife because she shares his family record, turning a shared patronymic and surname into a parent link, reading QUAY as a research status, silently converting an Old Style date or padding an approximate year, culling or confirming a supplied tree's claims during a format change, and marking people deceased so that they can go into a shared file.

GED-01.quote: **Never mark anyone deceased from a birth-year cutoff or a missing death date** in order to export, share or publish them.

GED-02.quote: **Apply the living-person rules to a copy prepared for sharing.**

GED-03.quote: **Never map QUAY to or from a research status.**

GED-04.quote: For an online destination, identify living or possibly living people and keep the upload conditional on each one's explicit permission for that destination or on leaving that person out completely (section 8).

GED-05.quote: A supplied `QUAY 3` and a source title or research note saying "unverified" are not contradictory merely because of that research-status wording.

GEDMATCH-PRACTICAL-DNA-WORKFLOWS-01.quote: A match-list row, a pairwise segment, a shared-match list, a triangulation result and a generated kit answer different questions. Keep their tool, inputs and settings attached to every result.

GM-01.quote: Authorization to analyze a kit is not permission to upload it.

GM-02.quote: require that person's explicit permission for GEDmatch and the chosen option.

GM-03.quote: For an upload request, make the gate explicit in the first reply: ask whether the file is the user's own test or someone else's, distinguish permission to access or analyze it from permission to transfer it, and ask about permission for GEDmatch and the chosen visibility and law-enforcement matching options.

GENEALOGICAL-NUMBERING-SYSTEMS-01.quote: Find the compiler's key or introduction and name the system before decoding a single number.

GENEALOGICAL-NUMBERING-SYSTEMS-02.quote: Take person 1's sex from the records, not from the number.

GENEALOGICAL-NUMBERING-SYSTEMS-03.quote: Read 11 as two positions, one and one, never as eleven.

GENEALOGICAL-NUMBERING-SYSTEMS-04.quote: Never decode a letter or bracket in a Henry number until the document's key says which child position it stands for.

GENEALOGICAL-NUMBERING-SYSTEMS-05.quote: Do not read a child without an identification number as childless or as dying young.

GENEALOGICAL-NUMBERING-SYSTEMS-06.quote: So decide continuation by the plus sign, never by the presence of a number.

GENEALOGY-STANDARDS-AUDIT-01.quote: A populated log, polished footnote or completed checklist does not establish the Genealogical Proof Standard (GPS). The researcher owns the final ruling on evidentiary sufficiency.

GENI-PRACTICAL-RESEARCH-WORKFLOWS-01.quote: Distinguish tree assertions, source-supported statements, pending requests and completed changes. Draft any manager or curator request for my review; do not send it.

GEORGIA-TEXAS-STATE-LAND-GRANT-RECOVERY-.quote: Do not read a missing name in a later lottery as proof that the person did not register, was not eligible or was not a resident.

GERMAN-COMPENSATION-FILE-RECOVERY-01.quote: The hit tells you a file exists for one indexed applicant or injured party. It does not tell you who filed the claim, which relatives the file names, or whether the indexed person is yours.

GERMAN-EMIGRANT-ORIGIN-SOURCES-01.quote: The main mistake to avoid is treating a miss in official emigration-permission files or a regional index as proof that the person did not come from that state.

GERMAN-LOCAL-CENSUS-REGISTRATION-RECOVER.quote: "No census here" ends that route only. Follow it with the other headings and the next archive.

GERMAN-MILITARY-RECORD-PERIOD-ROUTING-01.quote: A regimental canton, a gazette notice or a casualty-list line is a lead with limits. None of them is a birthplace, a death date or an identity.

GERMAN-OFFICIAL-GAZETTE-NOTICE-SEARCH-01.quote: Each notice is a dated act by a named authority. It does not show that the person lived in the gazette's district. It does not prove that anyone left, and it does not confirm anyone's identity.

GERMAN-REGISTER-IMAGE-RECOVERY-01.quote: **Narrow by the Kreis, Oberamt or state nesting.** Many towns share a name.

HEBREWBOOKS-SEARCH-RECOVERY-01.quote: An access error, an unsubmitted query and a completed search with zero hits are different observations. Record the surface and the observation before interpreting it.

HISPANIC-CATHOLIC-REGISTER-RECOVERY-01.quote: **Never copy a baptism date into the birth field.** Baptism could be late because of distance, the priest's fee or inertia [S2].

HISTORIC-HUNGARY-RECORD-ROUTING-01.quote: **For local registers outside today's Hungary, start with the successor state's archive.** Inside Hungary, check the parish for pre-1895 church books, the MNL in Budapest for films of those books [S20 @2026-11-16], and the county archive for second copies [S21 @2026-11-16].

HISTORICAL-MAP-RECORD-RECOVERY-01.quote: retain the map-to-case link as a candidate until the records establish it. Keep the estimated map-production date, the case-file span and any dated event statements separate. Seek the case's actual statements before dating the depicted event or moving a same-named person to another generation.

HISTORICAL-NEWSPAPER-SECTION-SEARCH-01.quote: Choose the section that fits the question before rerunning the name search.

HISTORICAL-PLACE-NAME-RESOLUTION-01.quote: The recipe lists every same-named feature in feature-level, period-dated gazetteers, keeps the name exactly as written, and lets other dated evidence about the person choose among the candidates.

HOLOCAUST-TESTIMONY-SOURCE-INTERPRETATIO.quote: Recover the information behind a Yad Vashem name result without converting a memorial submission, archival list or evacuation entry into an unsupported death or family conclusion.

ILLEGITIMACY-RECORD-RECOVERY-01.quote: A bond, court file or church-court suit records an accusation, a reputation or a court outcome. It does not prove biological fatherhood.

IMMIGRANT-CONGREGATION-ORIGIN-RECORDS-01.quote: One hometown statement in one entry is a lead. Before filing identity, correlate it with the rest of the family's evidence and with origin-side records.

INSTITUTIONAL-PATIENT-RECORD-RECOVERY-01.quote: Never treat a refusal, a form letter or a court-order requirement as evidence that no file exists. Log it as an access outcome and switch to the court and newspaper routes below.

INTERPRETING-ANCESTRY-COMPOSITION-ESTIMA.quote: An ethnicity estimate is a lead about where DNA resembles reference populations, not proof of any ancestor, origin or relationship.
A share of a few percent is a question, not a finding.
Do not reject a documented German line because the German-labelled category is low or missing.
Never use the size of a percentage difference between relatives as evidence for or against a relationship.
Never average calculators, or a calculator and a company estimate, and never choose the calculator whose result fits the expectation.
Record it as a parentage lead, not a conclusion, and keep it private.

IRISH-1901-1911-CENSUS-RETURNS-01.quote: Only a townland that has returns, searched by all the routes in steps 1–2 and browsed house by house, supports "not found in [townland], [year]".

IRISH-CATHOLIC-PARISH-IMAGE-RECOVERY-01.quote: Carry an Irish Catholic baptism or marriage lead into the National Library of Ireland's register images, inspect the actual entry and preserve the register and image locators. A transcription can identify a parish and date without supplying an image; a baptism date remains a baptism date unless the original separately records birth.

IRISH-CIVIL-REGISTRATION-JURISDICTION-RE.quote: Births are registered after they happen, so put the quarter in its own field. Take the event date only from the certificate.

IRISH-EMIGRANT-ORIGIN-LOCALITY-01.quote: Do not record a townland as the origin on a place-name, surname-distribution or farm-name match alone. Submit the person-specific evidence that ties this person to the townland, from destination or Irish records, and leave the identity ruling to the researcher.

IRISH-LAND-VALUATION-OCCUPANCY-SERIES-01.quote: Read each one as a dated list of occupiers and holdings. None of them is a household census.

IRISH-PROBATE-AND-DEED-RECOVERY-01.quote: **Do not read an entry as proof that the will survives.** The entry records the grant, not the document's survival; check the copy lanes in step 3.

ISRAEL-IMMIGRATION-LIST-RESEARCH-01.quote: Call the entry an immigration only when the list heading or the category column says the person arrived as an immigrant.

ISRAEL-IMMIGRATION-LIST-RESEARCH-02.quote: Do not stop at an English miss.

ISRAEL-IMMIGRATION-LIST-RESEARCH-03.quote: A miss means only that no surviving, indexed list matched your search.

ITALIAN-STATO-CIVILE-PARISH-RECORD-RECOV.quote: Fix who registered the event before you choose a series. Use the event year and the place's ruler in that year, not today's region.

JAPANESE-KOSEKI-HONSEKI-RECOVERY-01.quote: One spoken reading can be written with many kanji combinations, so a romanized name does not identify the person. The request needs the exact registered Japanese spelling, kanji or kana as recorded ([Kagoshima City naming FAQ](https://www.city.kagoshima.lg.jp/faq-kurashi/shimin/q113.html)).

JEWISH-ARCHIVAL-LIST-TRIAGE-01.quote: A geographical association does not establish either Jewish contents or the identity of a person. Do not present a title match as a verified Jewish list.

JEWISH-GENEALOGY-CONDITIONAL-HYPOTHESES-.quote: A proposed father can select a search town; establishing that father still does not establish the child's birthplace, the intended namesake or the ancestor behind every shared segment.

JEWISHGEN-SEARCH-FAMILY-RECONSTRUCTION-0.quote: Do not convert a phonetic, household or age match into a relationship.

LAND-INDEX-BOOK-SERIES-RECOVERY-01.quote: Keep both index directions, the instrument and recording dates, and the original locator visible, so one missed surname entry or guessed book does not become a false absence.

LITHUANIAN-JEWISH-HOUSEHOLD-REGISTERS-01.quote: Check the locality and register coverage before interpreting a name miss.

LOCAL-REPOSITORY-UNCATALOGUED-HOLDINGS-0.quote: Treat an empty catalogue or online search as covering only the repository's processed, catalogued holdings. Do not write "not held", "nothing found" or "searched [repository]" on the strength of it.

MAIDEN-NAME-RECOVERY-01.quote: A bride's surname on a marriage record is the name she used at that marriage.

MAIDEN-NAME-RECOVERY-02.quote: Search her Italian civil records under her maiden name, never only under her husband's surname.

MAIDEN-NAME-RECOVERY-03.quote: Read a name such as Leung Shee as a woman surnamed Leung, not as a given name.

MAIDEN-NAME-RECOVERY-04.quote: Do not treat a miss as evidence that she never applied.

MAIDEN-NAME-RECOVERY-05.quote: keep the request an unsent draft on the user's device until every item is answered

MANUSCRIPT-COLLECTION-RECOVERY-01.quote: A personal-name search that finds nothing is therefore not a finding. Never report "no manuscripts exist" or "not in this archive" because a name search failed [S1], [S3], [S21].

MARKS-AND-BRANDS-RECORD-RECOVERY-01.quote: Read the index headings and arrangement before searching by the owner's surname. A design initial can be the filing key: the teaching example finds an owner under the letter beginning the brand, rather than the owner's surname.

MAYFLOWER-AND-GREAT-MIGRATION-GENEALOGIE.quote: Select any Silver Books volume by passenger, child and generation.

MEMORIAL-CARD-AND-COFFIN-PLATE-EVIDENCE-.quote: The object points to those records; it does not replace them.
Its birth details were supplied then, by someone other than the person born, and are not a birth record.
A coffin plate kept by the family is not burial evidence.
Treat them as living and keep their names in the private research log.

MISSING-MARRIAGE-JURISDICTION-SEARCH-01.quote: A verified original that resolves the marriage ends the search. Otherwise the search is not finished, and the gap is not reported, until every ranked candidate has been searched or recorded as unavailable.

MUSCOVITE-CENSUS-SETTLER-ORIGIN-RECOVERY.quote: Every stated origin is kept as testimony until a matching departure-side entry is found.

MYHERITAGE-DNA-MATCH-INVESTIGATION-01.quote: Save empty results with their actual query, kit, filters and date. Do not fill an unshown DNA measurement with zero or infer that a person outside the list has no shared DNA.

MYHERITAGE-HISTORICAL-RECORD-SEARCH-01.quote: Preserve the sparse baseline before tightening it. If a tighter query fails, relax one condition at a time and record the reason; changing everything together conceals what excluded the record.

MYHERITAGE-KIT-PROCESSING-AND-DOWNLOADS-.quote: Identify the kit’s processing method from the file header before interpreting it.

MYHERITAGE-PROFILE-HINT-EXTRACTION-01.quote: Decide which facts the source supports before selecting any arrows.

NAZI-ERA-ANCESTRY-PROOF-RECORDS-01.quote: Their racial categories are the regime's classifications and are never evidence of anything about a person. Their entries were copied from parish and civil registers and must be checked against those registers.

NEW-YORK-CITY-VITAL-CERTIFICATE-EXTRACTI.quote: Search both filing series separately for a New York City marriage dated 1908–1937.

NEWSPAPERS-COM-SEARCH-RECOVERY-01.quote: A surname can occur in one item and a travel verb in another on the same page. Confirm the subject and event within the actual item before assigning that event to the searched person.

OLD-BELIEVER-SECTARIAN-RECORD-RECOVERY-0.quote: Use this recipe when a Russian-Empire family suspected of Old Belief (раскол, старообрядчество) or Edinoverie (единоверие) is missing from the ordinary Orthodox metrical books, revision lists or confession rolls.
